Reviewer concern: Reviewer 1: The data augmentation procedure appears to have been applied prior to train/test partitioning, raising severe concerns regarding data leakage and overly optimistic performance estimates.
Scientific issue: Data leakage: synthetic descendants (1% Gaussian noise clones) of test samples present in training partitions artificially inflate R2 and minimize prediction error.
Required analysis or experiment: Isolate original observations, establish strict partition boundaries before transformation, re-train models, and compare leaked vs. leakage-free holdout metrics.
Work actually completed: Implemented 01_leakage_safe_pipeline.py: assigned unique parent IDs, split original 256 rows (80/20), augmented train partition only, and tested on untouched original holdout rows.
Actual result: Empirically verified that 90.9% to 96.9% of test rows had twins in training under original split. Clean test R2 dropped from 0.85 to 0.31 in Room Temp; unified model achieved clean R2=0.7587.
Proposed manuscript modification: [Requires Author Verification] Replace all inflated R2 > 0.90 tables with leakage-safe benchmarks. Add Section 3.2 detailing the data-leakage audit and comparing leaked vs. corrected metrics.
Remaining limitation: Sample size of clean test sets is constrained (N=11 for Cryo, N=9 for High, N=32 for Room, N=52 for Unified Combined).
Draft response to reviewer: We thank the reviewer for this critical methodological observation. We conducted a comprehensive audit and confirmed that pre-split augmentation caused severe data leakage. We have completely restructured our pipeline: train/test partitioning was executed strictly on original physical observations before any augmentation. In the revised manuscript, we present transparent comparisons between the leaked and corrected models, establishing defensible baseline metrics.

Reviewer concern: Reviewer 2: The manuscript claims general applicability to space-grade composites, but does the model genuinely generalize to unseen composite material systems and novel filler chemistries?
Scientific issue: Cross-material transferability: empirical tabular regressors trained without microstructural descriptors (aspect ratio, surface functionalization, Kapitza resistance) cannot extrapolate across material classes.
Required analysis or experiment: Execute Grouped Cross-Validation (GroupKFold) grouping observations by filler material family to test predictive capability on withheld material classes.
Work actually completed: Executed 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation across all filler material classes (Al2O3, Cu, TiO2, AlN, CNTs, Graphite, Diamond, Polymer Beads, SS304).
Actual result: Mean GroupKFold R2 plummeted to -0.0703 (+/- 0.5665), indicating that empirical tree models fail to predict composite conductivity for unseen filler chemistries without direct training examples.
Proposed manuscript modification: [Requires Author Verification] Narrow the scope of claims: explicitly retract 'universal applicability to arbitrary composites' and clarify that the model functions as an interpolative tool within known material families.
Remaining limitation: Predictive transfer to entirely new filler classes requires microscopic morphological descriptors (particle size, aspect ratio, interfacial thermal resistance).
Draft response to reviewer: We fully agree with the reviewer. To rigorously assess generalizability to unseen composite systems, we implemented Grouped 5-Fold Cross-Validation by filler chemistry. As documented in Section 4.3 and Table 4, the mean R2 across unseen filler families drops to -0.0703, demonstrating that empirical models lacking microstructural descriptors cannot reliably extrapolate to novel filler chemistries. We have substantially revised our claims to emphasize this limitation.

Reviewer concern: Reviewer 3: The dataset combines cryogenic, room, and elevated temperature conditions, but what are the exact sources, material identities, and physical consistency across these regimes?
Scientific issue: Data provenance and consistency: datasets compiled from disparate secondary literature may mix incompatible material systems, such as liquid nanofluids and solid cross-linked polymers.
Required analysis or experiment: Perform full data provenance audit: classify matrix and filler identities, temperature ranges, and material phase for every observation. Check for duplicate and overlapping rows.
Work actually completed: Implemented 02_data_provenance.py: classified all 256 physical observations, audited temperature distributions, and mapped material phases across Cryogenic, High, and Room regimes.
Actual result: Discovered that 25 of 42 rows (59.5%) in High Temp are liquid water-based nanofluids (Base TC = 0.60-0.68 W/mK), not solid epoxy composites. SS304 appears only once across the entire 256-row dataset.
Proposed manuscript modification: [Requires Author Verification] Disclose dataset composition transparently in Section 2.1; clarify the distinction between solid polymer composites and liquid nanofluid literature benchmarks.
Remaining limitation: Original literature sources for some secondary compiled rows remain unconfirmed in the supplied files.
Draft response to reviewer: The reviewer raises an essential question regarding dataset provenance. Our comprehensive provenance audit revealed that the elevated-temperature dataset compiled from secondary literature contained 25 water-based nanofluid observations alongside solid composites. Furthermore, SS304 was present in only one physical observation in the training corpus. We have revised Section 2 to transparently document the exact provenance, material phases, and distributions across all three temperature regimes.

Reviewer concern: Reviewer 4: The authors claim experimental validation, but no details of composite fabrication, measurement instrumentation, uncertainty, or calibration standards are provided.
Scientific issue: Experimental rigor vs. theoretical calculation: conflating analytical mixture models (Maxwell equation) with physical experimental measurements violates scientific reporting standards.
Required analysis or experiment: Inspect supplied validation files (4.2K.docx, 300K.docx, 323K.docx), verify measurement methodology, compare ML predictions against reference values, and identify discrepancies.
Work actually completed: Implemented 05_external_validation.py: audited all three docx files, extracted mathematical formulas, computed ML vs. Maxwell discrepancies, and analyzed Thermal Boundary Resistance (TBR) effects.
Actual result: Proved that 4.2K.docx, 300K.docx, and 323K.docx contain theoretical Maxwell calculations with TBR corrections, NOT experimental measurements. ML predictions deviate from Maxwell benchmarks by up to 48.8%.
Proposed manuscript modification: [Requires Author Verification] Retract claims of 'experimental validation'. Reframe Section 5 as 'Comparison with Analytical Micromechanical Models (Maxwell-Garnett Theory)'. Outline a prospective experimental testing plan.
Remaining limitation: Physical experimental testing using calibrated Hot Disk or laser flash apparatus has not yet been conducted by the authors.
Draft response to reviewer: We appreciate the reviewer highlighting this crucial distinction. Our audit revealed that the validation files supplied were theoretical calculations derived from the classical Maxwell mixture model incorporating Thermal Boundary Resistance adjustments, rather than physical experimental measurements. We have formally retracted claims of experimental validation in the revised manuscript and reframed this analysis as an evaluative comparison against analytical effective medium theory.

Reviewer concern: Reviewer 5: Claims regarding space-grade materials, universal predictive superiority, and broad temperature applicability appear overstated relative to the available evidence.
Scientific issue: Scientific claim overreach: asserting broad technological readiness (space-grade qualification) without corroborating physical test data (outgassing, thermal cycling).
Required analysis or experiment: Audit all major claims against empirical evidence; classify claims as supported, partially supported, or unsupported; formulate defensible scientific alternatives.
Work actually completed: Conducted systematic scientific claims audit in scientific_claims_audit.md, classifying all 6 primary manuscript assertions and providing precise, defensible rewrites.
Actual result: Identified that claims of 'space-grade qualification', 'universal accuracy (R2 > 0.90)', and 'broad generalisation' were unsupported by the empirical data and required strict narrowing.
Proposed manuscript modification: [Requires Author Verification] Implement recommended revisions in Title, Abstract, Introduction, and Conclusion to align scope with verifiable empirical findings.
Remaining limitation: Long-term environmental durability and space-qualification metrics remain beyond the scope of tabular regression models.
Draft response to reviewer: We thank the reviewer for urging scientific precision. We have conducted a thorough claims audit and substantially revised the manuscript to eliminate overstated assertions. References to 'space-grade composites' and 'universal applicability' have been replaced with precise descriptions of empirical regression on compiled literature datasets across 2 to 423 K. We explicitly discuss the physical limitations of the approach in Section 5.
